Features: Which One Tells These Windows Apart?
after.scenario: Two synthetic 1-second windows at 8 samples per second. Window P is [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3] µV. Window Q is [3, -3, 3, -3, 3, -3, 3, -3] µV. You can compute the mean, the RMS and the count of samples at or above 4 µV.
after.signalDescription: Mean = sum / N. RMS = square root of (sum of squares / N). The count uses at or above 4 µV.
after.decisionQuestion: Which statement about the three features is correct?

choices.label: RMS separates them, because P is louder
choices.rationale: Every sample in both windows has size 3, so every square is 9 and both RMS values are 3 µV. RMS discards sign.

choices.label: None of the three separates them, because their RMS values match
choices.rationale: Equal RMS does not mean equal windows. The means differ: P averages 3 µV and Q averages 0 µV.

choices.label: The count at or above 4 µV separates them
choices.rationale: No sample in either window reaches 4 µV, so both counts are 0.

choices.label: Only the mean separates them: 3 µV versus 0 µV
choices.rationale: P sums to 24 over 8 samples, mean 3 µV; Q sums to 0, mean 0 µV. Both RMS values are 3 µV and both counts are 0. A constant offset like P's is also what electrode drift looks like, so a feature that depends on it needs checking against drift.

after.oneLineMaster: Each feature keeps one property of a window; check which property actually differs.

after.title: Population: One Channel Goes Quiet
after.scenario: Four synthetic channels prefer right, up, left and down, each with a 10 Hz baseline. The decoded direction is x = right minus left modulation and y = up minus down modulation. During an intended upward move the rates were [10, 30, 10, 0] Hz. The next day the "up" channel stays at 10 Hz whatever the user does; the other three behave as before.
after.signalDescription: Yesterday's modulations: [0, +20, 0, -10] Hz. Today the up channel's modulation is 0.
after.decisionQuestion: With the same fixed readout, what does an intended upward move decode to today?

choices.label: A zero vector: the move cannot be decoded
choices.rationale: The down channel still drops 10 Hz below baseline, so y = 0 - (-10) = 10. One silent channel does not remove the others' votes.

choices.label: A downward vector
choices.rationale: Losing an upward vote cannot reverse the sign here: the remaining down channel still votes against down.

choices.label: Still upward, at half yesterday's length: (0, 10) instead of (0, 30)
choices.rationale: Yesterday y = 20 - (-10) = 30. Today y = 0 - (-10) = 10, x stays 0. The direction survives and the magnitude shrinks: graceful degradation from redundancy.

choices.label: A rightward vector
choices.rationale: The right and left channels are both at baseline, so x = 0 - 0 = 0.

choices.label: The trial at 5 s [10, 10]: a zero score is labeled right
choices.rationale: A score of 0 is not above 0, so the tie rule gives left, which matches the label.

choices.label: None; all six are labeled correctly
choices.rationale: Check each score against its label: one right-labeled trial has a negative score.

choices.rationale: f1 - f0 = 11 - 12 = -1, so the rule says left. This trial sits just on the wrong side of the boundary. Moving the boundary to fix it would change other trials too.

choices.label: The trial at 1 s [14, 6]: score -8 gives right

after.scenario: Four synthetic training rows [f0, f1, label]: [2, 6, right], [7, 3, left], [5, 6, right], [6, 4, left]. Bias 0; right only when the score is above 0. Candidate weights: [-1, 1], [1, -1], [0, 1] and [-1, 0.5].

after.decisionQuestion: Which choice and claim are supported?

choices.label: [0, 1], because ignoring f0 will generalize best
choices.rationale: With only f1, every score is positive, so it labels all four rows right and gets 2/4. Ignoring a feature is not evidence of better generalization.

choices.label: [-1, 1] fits all four training rows; accuracy on new trials is still unknown
choices.rationale: Scores are 4, -4, 1 and -2, all on the correct side. Four training rows support the choice of weights, not a claim about new trials: that needs held-out data scored once.

choices.label: [-1, 0.5], because smaller weights always generalize better
choices.rationale: It gets 3/4: row 3 scores -5 + 3 = -2. Regularization can help, but smaller is not automatically better.

choices.label: [-1, 1] fits all four rows, so it will be 100 % accurate on new trials
choices.rationale: The training fit is right, but four rows cannot establish performance on future trials.

after.title: Cursor: Why Is the Start So Steady?
after.scenario: A toy cursor starts at 0 with a target at 1. Each 0.1 s update sets velocity = 8 × (target - position), clips it to a 2 units/s speed limit, and moves by velocity × 0.1. There is no delay and no noise.
after.signalDescription: Positions every 0.1 s: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.96, 0.992, 0.9984, 0.99968. The first command is 8 × 1 = 8 units/s.
after.decisionQuestion: Why does the cursor move in equal 0.2-unit steps at first and then slow down?

choices.label: The speed limit clips the large early commands to 2 units/s; near the target the command falls below the limit
choices.rationale: 8 × 1 = 8 is clipped to 2, so each step is 2 × 0.1 = 0.2. At 0.8 the command is 8 × 0.2 = 1.6, under the limit, so steps shrink as the error shrinks.

choices.label: Delay: the cursor sees an old position
choices.rationale: This model has no delay; each update uses the current position.

choices.label: The decoder is noisy at the start
choices.rationale: The model is deterministic. Equal steps come from a rule, not from noise.

choices.label: The gain of 8 is too low to move faster
choices.rationale: An unclipped command of 8 units/s would cover 0.8 units in the first step. The limit, not the gain, sets the early speed.

after.oneLineMaster: A speed limit makes large commands equal; small commands near the target pass through unchanged.

after.title: Latency: Why Does the Cursor Overshoot?
after.scenario: A toy loop moves a cursor toward a target at 1.0. Every 0.1 s it sets velocity = 5 × (target - observed position) and moves by velocity × 0.1. The speed limit, 10 units/s, is never reached. In the plotted run the observed position is 0.2 s old.
after.decisionQuestion: The two runs share the target, gain and speed limit. What explains the overshoot?

choices.label: The speed limit is too low
choices.rationale: Velocities never exceed 5 units/s, half the limit, so clipping plays no part.

choices.label: Decoder noise
choices.rationale: The model has no noise: the same inputs always give the same trajectory.

choices.label: A higher gain in the delayed run
choices.rationale: Both runs use gain 5; only the age of the observed position differs.

choices.label: Corrections use a position 0.2 s old, so they keep pushing after the cursor has passed the target
choices.rationale: At 0.2 s the cursor is at 1.0, but the loop still sees 0 and adds another 0.5. By the time it sees the overshoot, it is already at 1.75. Lowering the gain or the delay reduces the swing.

after.title: Recalibration: What Is the Smallest Fix?
after.scenario: A six-channel synthetic decoder normalizes each feature as (value - resting mean) / scale and keeps its weights fixed. Today's resting means match yesterday's within 1 Hz on all channels. In a 20-trial block with known targets, channel 4's reach-minus-rest change is 9 Hz, versus 18 Hz yesterday; its preferred direction is unchanged. The other five channels match yesterday.
after.signalDescription: Channel 4 scale: 18 Hz yesterday; the cued block suggests 9 Hz today. Offsets unchanged.
after.decisionQuestion: What is the best first recalibration step?

choices.label: Re-estimate every resting mean from a rest block
choices.rationale: Resting means already match, so new offsets would change almost nothing.

choices.label: Refit all the weights from a full calibration session
choices.rationale: This would work, but it costs the user a full session when one parameter explains the change. Keep it as the fallback.

choices.label: Update channel 4's scale to 9 Hz, keep the weights, and re-test
choices.rationale: Only channel 4's modulation halved, and its direction is unchanged. Halving its scale restores its normalized range with the least change; re-testing shows whether anything else moved.

choices.label: Drop channel 4 from the decoder
choices.rationale: Channel 4 still carries half its modulation. Dropping it discards information a scale update can recover.

after.oneLineMaster: Match the fix to the signature: a gain change on one channel needs that channel's scale, not a new decoder.

after.scenario: A synthetic decoder scores four windows per second, threshold 0, and abstains when a score is within 0.5 of 0. After three confident windows, the next nine scores all fall inside the margin, so the cursor has held still for 2.25 s.

choices.label: Shrink the margin to 0 so the cursor moves again
choices.rationale: That hides the uncertainty and lets the weakest evidence drive actions, which is when errors are most likely.

choices.label: Keep holding, show that the system is unsure, and offer a quick recalibration or another input
choices.rationale: The user learns why nothing is happening and gets a way forward. The decoder does not act on evidence it has already judged too weak.

choices.rationale: The confident windows are more than two seconds old; acting on them ignores what the user is doing now.

choices.label: Silently reset the decoder weights
choices.rationale: An unannounced change can make control feel different without explanation and may not address the cause.

after.title: Safety: Price the Errors, Then Choose
after.scenario: A synthetic closed-loop detector was run on one recorded day with three settings. A: threshold 5, act on 1 window: 30 false actions, 0 missed events. B: threshold 5, act after 3 consecutive 100 ms windows: 4 false actions, 1 missed event, 200 ms added delay. C: threshold 8, act on 1 window: 2 false actions, 4 missed events. The team agreed a false action costs 1, a missed event costs 8, and events last at least 2 s, so 200 ms of delay is acceptable.
after.signalDescription: The plot shows a short excerpt at 10 Hz with threshold 5: a single-window artifact at index 2 and a sustained event from index 5. Circles mark where setting A would act.
after.decisionQuestion: Which setting has the lowest agreed cost?

choices.label: A: it never misses an event
choices.rationale: A costs 30 × 1 + 0 × 8 = 30. Never missing is valuable, but 30 false actions cost more here.

choices.label: C: it has the fewest false actions
choices.rationale: C costs 2 × 1 + 4 × 8 = 34. Its missed events are the most expensive error.

choices.label: All three cost the same
choices.rationale: They cost 30, 12 and 34.

choices.label: B: 4 × 1 + 1 × 8 = 12, with an acceptable delay
choices.rationale: Confirmation removed most false actions, including the single-window artifact in the excerpt, at the cost of one missed event and 200 ms of delay that this application can tolerate.

after.oneLineMaster: Choose the operating point by agreed costs, and check that any added delay fits the application.

after.title: Graded Speed: Slow Down When Unsure
after.neuroengineeringConcept: Showing decoder uncertainty in the interface
after.explanation: Instead of jumping between full speed and a stop, the cursor speed can grow with the score's distance from the threshold, reaching full speed at the margin. The user sees the cursor slow as the evidence weakens. Direction follows the sign of score minus threshold; exactly at the threshold the speed is zero.
after.challengePrompt: Define graded_speed(score, threshold, margin, full_speed). Let d = score - threshold. Return full_speed × min(1, |d| / margin), positive when d > 0 and negative when d < 0 (zero when d is zero). Raise ValueError when margin is zero or negative, or full_speed is negative.
after.hint: Compute the unsigned speed first, then return its negative when d < 0.
after.solution:
def graded_speed(score, threshold, margin, full_speed):
    if margin <= 0 or full_speed < 0:
        raise ValueError("margin must be positive and full_speed non-negative")
    d = score - threshold
    speed = full_speed * min(1, abs(d) / margin)
    return -speed if d < 0 else speed

print(graded_speed(0.1, 0, 0.5, 4))

changes.before: Feature extraction is where raw neural data becomes model-ready evidence. A good feature set often beats a fancier model on bad features.
changes.after: A decoder never sees the raw trace. It sees the few numbers you chose to compute from each window, so anything those numbers discard is invisible to every later stage.

changes.before: A feature vector is a small set of numbers that summarize the neural evidence relevant to the task. Common useful features include spike count in a window, root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude, and band-power proxies. The decoder will later see only these numbers, not the raw trace.
changes.after: A feature is a number computed from a window of samples; a feature vector is the short list of such numbers passed to a decoder. Each feature keeps one property of the window and throws the rest away. The mean keeps the signed average level, so a constant offset changes it. Root mean square (RMS) is the square root of the mean of the squared samples. It keeps overall size and discards sign, so it is never negative. A threshold count, such as the number of samples at or above a level, keeps whether large values occurred but not their exact size or timing. All three carry the input units except the count, which is dimensionless. Two windows can share a mean and an RMS yet differ in ways a decoder needs, such as one brief large deflection versus a steady oscillation. Choosing features is therefore a choice about which differences you believe matter for the task. A feature that separates training windows is a candidate, not evidence of a neural cause: an offset from electrode drift or an artifact correlated with the task can separate windows just as well.

changes.before: The raw voltage trace is a long movie. A feature vector is the short list of answers to the questions the decoder actually cares about right now.
changes.after: Each feature is a question you ask the window. Mean asks "where is the average level?", RMS asks "how big is it overall?", a count asks "how often did it get large?". The decoder can only use the answers, never the window.

changes.before: In a 200 ms window you compute: spike_count = 4, rms = 12.3, beta_power_proxy = 0.7. These three numbers become the input vector [4, 12.3, 0.7] for the decoder.
changes.after: Two synthetic 10-sample windows in microvolts. Window A: [1, 0, -1, 10, -5, -5, 2, 0, -2, 0]. Window B: [4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4]. Both sums are 0, so both means are 0 µV. Squares in A add to 1 + 1 + 100 + 25 + 25 + 4 + 4 = 160; every square in B is 16, also 160 in total. Both RMS values are the square root of 160 / 10 = 16, which is 4 µV. Counting samples at or above +8 µV gives 1 for A (the 10) and 0 for B. Mean and RMS cannot tell these windows apart; the count can. Whether that count reflects neural activity is a separate question this calculation does not answer.

changes.before: RMS captures overall signal strength (energy) rather than being dominated by one outlier sample.

changes.before: A linear decoder is the simplest model that actually learns from data. Understanding weighted sums, bias, and evaluation on held-out data is the foundation of almost every production BCI decoder.
changes.after: A decoder is the step where numbers become a command. Writing that step as an explicit rule lets you trace every output back to the features, weights and tie rule that produced it.

changes.before: A linear decoder computes a score = w₁·f₁ + w₂·f₂ + … + b, then applies a decision rule (threshold or argmax). The weights are the learned 'importance' of each feature. Good weights turn noisy population activity into a reliable command.
changes.after: The simplest decoder computes a score from the feature vector and compares it with zero. A linear score multiplies each feature by a weight, adds the products and adds a bias: score = w0·f0 + w1·f1 + b. A positive score maps to one label and everything else to the other. The set of feature vectors where the score is exactly zero is the decision boundary; for two features it is a straight line. Weights set the boundary's orientation and the bias shifts it. Three details decide whether the rule is fully specified. First, the tie rule: what happens at exactly zero. Without one, two programs can disagree on the same input. Second, the sign convention: "right" for positive scores is an engineering choice, not a property of the brain. Flipping every weight and the bias swaps the labels. Third, units: each weight is in label-score units per feature unit, so changing a feature from hertz to spikes per window changes the weight needed. A rule that labels training rows well has learned a boundary for those rows. Whether it holds on new trials is a separate test (Unit 10 in this module).

changes.before: Each feature votes with a strength (its weight). The total vote plus bias decides the output. Changing one weight visibly changes behavior.
changes.after: Draw the two features as axes. The decoder is a straight fence across that plane. Points on one side get one label; points on the fence itself go wherever the tie rule sends them.

changes.before: Features = [spike_count_left=5, spike_count_right=12]. With weights w_left=-0.8, w_right=+1.1 and bias=-1.0 the score is 5.4. Positive score → 'right'. If you flip the weights the decoder inverts.
changes.after: Features are a left-channel rate f0 and a right-channel rate f1, in Hz. Weights [-1, 1] and bias 0 give score = f1 - f0, labeled right when the score is above 0. Trial [12, 20]: score 8, right. Trial [18, 9]: score -9, left. Trial [15, 15]: score 0, left by the tie rule. Now set the bias to -5, so right needs f1 - f0 above 5. Trial [12, 20] scores 8 - 5 = 3 and stays right. Trial [14, 17] scores 3 - 5 = -2 and becomes left. The bias moved the fence 5 Hz toward the right-channel side. All rates are invented.

changes.before: Why is a weighted sum more powerful than a single if-statement on one feature?
changes.after: Why does a decoder need an explicit tie rule?

changes.before: It can combine evidence and cancel noise.
changes.after: Think about a score of exactly zero.

changes.before: It lets the decoder listen to the whole population and automatically down-weight unreliable channels.
changes.after: Without one, the label for a zero score depends on how the comparison happens to be written, so two implementations can disagree on the same input.

changes.before: What does it mean when a decoder performs well on training trials but poorly on new 'held-out' trials?
changes.after: What happens to every label if you multiply both weights and the bias by -1?

changes.before: It memorized noise instead of the real pattern.
changes.after: Each score changes sign.

changes.before: It overfit. The weights captured quirks of the training set that do not generalize.
changes.after: Every nonzero score flips sign, so right and left swap. Scores of exactly zero stay zero and keep the tie-rule label.

changes.before: Treating the decoder as a black box instead of inspecting which features have large positive or negative weights.
changes.after: Reading the decoder's "right" label as the person's intention, when it is a rule-defined label on synthetic or recorded features.

changes.before: You can write a tiny linear decoder (weighted sum + threshold), adjust the weights by hand, and explain why performance changed on both training and held-out examples.
changes.after: You can compute a linear score and label by hand, apply the tie rule, explain what weights and bias do to the decision boundary, and predict the effect of flipping signs.

changes.before: Cursor control shows the full BCI loop: neural signal, decoding, feedback, user adaptation, and recalibration.
changes.after: In a cursor BCI the decoder output is not the end of the pipeline. It moves something the user watches, and what the user sees shapes the next neural activity the decoder receives.

changes.before: A cursor-control BCI does not end at classification. The decoded command moves a cursor, the user sees feedback, and the next neural activity changes based on that feedback. Latency and feedback quality shape learning.
changes.after: Many intracortical cursor BCIs decode a velocity rather than a position; the high-performance decoder of Gilja and colleagues (2012) is one example. At each update the decoded velocity is multiplied by the update interval dt and added to the current position: x[t+1] = x[t] + v[t]·dt. Most systems clip the velocity to a maximum speed so that one noisy window cannot throw the cursor across the screen. The loop then closes through the person. They see where the cursor is, compare it with where they want it, and their next attempt changes the neural activity the decoder sees. This makes the system a feedback loop with a human in it. Three consequences follow. Errors in velocity accumulate into position, so a small constant bias becomes steady drift. The speed limit trades responsiveness for safety and smoothness. And the user adapts to the decoder while the engineer adapts the decoder to the user, so performance measured with one decoder version does not transfer automatically to another.

changes.before: Cursor BCI is a loop, not a line: brain to decoder to screen back to brain.
changes.after: The decoder is a steering wheel, not a teleport. It sets how fast the cursor moves for the next fraction of a second; the person watches and steers again.

changes.before: If the decoder outputs LEFT with 80% confidence, the cursor nudges left; if feedback is delayed, the user may overcorrect.

Step 2: 6 is clipped to 4, so 0.10 + 4 × 0.05 = 0.30. Step 3: 0.30 - 1 × 0.05 = 0.25. A constant decoding bias of 0.2 units/s while the user rests would add 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01 units every step, or 0.2 units every second. Reaching a target 1 unit away at the full 4 units/s takes 1 / 4 = 0.25 s, five updates of 0.05 s; with a 2 units/s limit it takes ten updates. Numbers are synthetic and the model has no delay; Unit 12 adds one.

changes.before: Calibration keeps the decoder aligned with neural signals that naturally change over time.
changes.after: The recorded signals change within a day and across days. A decoder calibrated yesterday can push the cursor somewhere the user did not intend today, and the cheapest fix depends on what kind of change happened.

changes.before: Decoder drift happens when the relationship between features and commands shifts. Causes include electrode movement, tissue response, changing attention, fatigue, or baseline firing shifts. Calibration checks whether today’s signals still match yesterday’s model.
changes.after: Calibration fits a decoder's parameters, such as each channel's baseline and the weights, using data recorded while the intended action is known. Drift is any later change in the relationship between features and intent. Perge and colleagues (2013) found that signal changes within a single day measurably reduced decoding performance in people with intracortical arrays. Causes include small electrode movements, tissue responses, changes in attention or fatigue, and changes in which neurons are near each electrode. Three simple drift signatures need different responses. An additive offset shifts a feature by a constant: rest and movement values both rise by the same amount. A gain change scales how much the feature moves with intent. A tuning change alters which direction or action a channel responds to. Subtracting the change in resting baseline corrects only the first. It needs a short rest block, no labels and little time, which is why it is often the first step. If the cursor stops drifting at rest but movements are still too small or point the wrong way, the remaining error is not an offset, and a calibration block with known targets is needed.

changes.before: Closed-loop systems can act automatically, so false positives and false negatives become safety problems, not just accuracy numbers.
changes.after: When a system acts on its own detections, error rates become events per day that someone experiences. A rule that looks accurate on paper can still act wrongly dozens of times a day.

changes.before: A closed-loop system senses, decides, acts, and updates. In neurotechnology, the action might be stimulation, feedback, or device adjustment. Designers must balance sensitivity, specificity, timing, and user control.
changes.after: A closed-loop neurotechnology system senses a signal, decides whether a condition is present, acts, and then senses again, so its own action can change what it measures next. Responsive neurostimulation for epilepsy is a clinical example: the implant detects programmed electrographic patterns and delivers brief stimulation (Morrell, 2011). Two error types matter. A false positive acts when the condition is absent; a false negative misses it. Sensitivity is the fraction of true events detected. Specificity is the fraction of non-events correctly ignored. The trap is base rate. A detector usually checks many short windows, and almost all of them are non-events. Even 99 % specificity then produces many false actions, and most actions may be false even though each one looked unlikely. The positive predictive value, the fraction of actions that were correct, falls as events become rarer. Designers therefore also gate actions with conditions that do not depend on the detector, such as a device being armed or a power supply being adequate, and they decide which error is worse before choosing a threshold.

changes.before: Closed loop is a thermostat with higher stakes: sense, decide, act, then sense again.
changes.after: A smoke alarm in a kitchen. It checks the air every second of every day; even a rare false alarm per check adds up to many false alarms per week. How often it checks and how rare real fires are matter as much as how good each single check is.

changes.before: If abnormal activity detection triggers stimulation too easily, false positives may stimulate when the user did not need it.
changes.after: A synthetic detector checks 10-second windows: 8,640 per day. 20 windows contain the target pattern; 8,620 do not. Sensitivity 90 % detects 0.9 × 20 = 18 events. Specificity 99 % still flags 1 % of 8,620, about 86 windows. Of roughly 104 actions, 18 are correct: a positive predictive value near 17 %. Raising specificity to 99.9 % cuts false actions to about 9, if sensitivity can be kept. A gating condition, such as acting only while the device is armed, leaves these detection counts unchanged; it limits when a detection may become an action. These counts are invented for practice.

changes.before: A BCI succeeds only if the person can understand, trust, and control the interaction over time.
changes.after: The person using a BCI learns from what the interface shows them. An interface that hides uncertainty or changes behavior silently makes the whole system harder to control, however good the decoder is.

changes.before: Human-centered BCI UX includes feedback, latency, fatigue, calibration transparency, confidence display, and autonomy. The interface helps the user learn the system and helps the system remain accountable to the user.
changes.after: The interface is part of the control loop. What it shows, and when, changes what the user tries next. Several design choices follow. Show uncertainty in a form the user can act on: slowing the cursor as the score approaches the threshold tells the user, without words, that the system is unsure, and invites a stronger or clearer attempt. Graded speed of this kind is a continuous cousin of the abstain rule in Unit 15. Make changes visible: when the system recalibrates or adapts, say so, say what changed, and allow it to be undone. Protect control: a stop or pause that works through a separate input should always be available, so a misbehaving decoder cannot trap the user. Respect fatigue: performance and comfort change across a session, and long calibrations cost the user's time and energy. Measure what matters to the user, such as correct selections per minute including the time spent undoing errors, not only decoder accuracy. Clinical BCI studies report outcomes like typing rates for this reason (Pandarinath et al., 2017). None of these choices make the decoder more accurate; they make the person and the system easier to coordinate.

changes.before: The UI is part of the neural circuit: it changes what the user tries next.
changes.after: The screen is a conversation, not a scoreboard. Every movement says something to the user about how sure the system is.

Score -0.3 gives -(4 × 0.6) = -2.4 units/s. Score 0.9 is beyond the margin and gives the full 4 units/s. At 0.8 units/s, crossing 1 unit takes 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 s, slow enough to notice. Throughput: 10 selections in 60 s with 2 wrong, each needing a 5 s undo, gives 8 correct in 60 s = 8 per minute; it is not 10.

changes.before: Brain data can be sensitive because it may reveal attention, intent, state, or patterns the user did not mean to share.
changes.after: Neural data can support inferences about attention, mood or health that the person never meant to share. What a system collects, keeps and passes on is a design decision made long before anyone misuses it.

changes.before: Brain data safety means collecting the minimum useful data, explaining what is collected, protecting it, and giving users control. Ethics is not a final slide; it shapes the system design from the beginning.
changes.after: Brain data raise the ordinary privacy questions with higher stakes. Recordings and the features computed from them can support inferences beyond their original purpose, and the person may not be able to tell what is being inferred. Ethicists have argued for explicit protections of mental privacy and agency (Yuste et al., 2017) and for rights specific to neurotechnology (Ienca and Andorno, 2017). Several practical principles follow, and some also appear in data-protection law such as the EU's GDPR. Purpose limitation: state what the data are for and use them only for that. Data minimization: collect and keep only what that purpose needs. Specific, revocable consent: the person agrees to particular uses, can understand them and can withdraw. Retention limits: delete what is no longer needed. Access control: limit and log who can see the data. Minimization is often a technical choice. Sending computed features instead of raw recordings cuts the data volume dramatically. Smaller is not automatically safe, though: features can still reveal states the person did not mean to share, so the purpose test applies to them too. A code filter that drops fields is one protective measure; it does not establish consent, anonymity or legal compliance by itself.

changes.before: Treat brain data like a private journal with timestamps and sensor metadata.
changes.after: Treat a neural recording like a diary that writes itself. Ask what each page is for before you keep it, and who else could read something you did not mean to say.

Features instead: 2 numbers per channel per 20 ms bin is 96 × 2 = 192 numbers per bin; 50 bins per second makes 9,600 numbers per second, × 4 bytes = 38,400 bytes per second. That is 150 times less data (5,760,000 / 38,400 = 150). The features still describe moment-to-moment activity on every channel, so they still need a stated purpose and consent.

changes.before: Modern high-channel implants record from hundreds to >1000 neurons simultaneously. The population vector (or its modern descendant: a compact feature vector across channels or sorted units) remains the fundamental representation almost every decoder consumes.
changes.after: Single channels are noisy and can stop working. Decoders combine many channels into one vector so that intent is read from the pattern across the population rather than from any one recording site.

changes.before: A population vector is the list of firing rates or feature values across the recorded population at one time step. In real systems the 'vector' is often per-channel or per-unit features plus LFP band powers; the decoder rarely sees raw spikes or voltage traces.
changes.after: A population vector, in the classic sense, comes from recordings in which each neuron fires most for one movement direction, its preferred direction. Each neuron votes for its preferred direction, weighted by how far its rate is above or below its own baseline; the sum of the votes points in the decoded direction. Georgopoulos and colleagues showed in 1986 that this sum tracked arm-movement direction in monkey motor cortex. Today the term is often used loosely for the feature vector: one number per channel or unit (a rate, a threshold-crossing count) at one time step. Most modern decoders apply learned weights to that vector rather than assuming a direction per neuron, but the idea is the same: a fixed linear combination across many channels. Combining channels helps because independent noise partly cancels. If each of N channels has independent noise with standard deviation s, their average has standard deviation s divided by the square root of N. Noise that is shared across channels, such as a common reference artifact, does not cancel this way. A population readout also degrades gradually: losing one channel shortens or bends the vector instead of erasing it.

changes.before: Each neuron is one noisy coordinate. The current evidence for intent is the entire short list of numbers. Classic cosine tuning and modern high-density arrays both reduce to this same idea: the pattern across the population carries the signal.
changes.after: Each channel is one noisy voter with a fixed direction. The vote is the sum of everyone's arrows. A few voters going quiet makes the result weaker, not random.

changes.before: On a 64-channel array you compute spike count + RMS in a 100 ms window per channel (or per sorted unit). The resulting ~128-element feature vector is what the linear decoder receives. Real pipelines often add a few LFP band-power features and then reduce dimensionality.
changes.after: Four synthetic channels prefer right, up, left and down. Each has a baseline of 10 Hz. One 100 ms window gives rates [30, 20, 10, 0] Hz, so the modulations are [+20, +10, 0, -10] Hz. Horizontal component: right minus left = 20 - 0 = 20. Vertical component: up minus down = 10 - (-10) = 20. The vector (20, 20) points up and to the right at 45 degrees. Noise: if each channel's rate had independent noise with standard deviation 4 Hz, the average of the four channels would have 4 / 2 = 2 Hz, because the square root of 4 is 2. These numbers are invented; real tuning is broader and noise is partly shared.

changes.before: Individual neurons are noisy and can drop out; the population average or weighted combination cancels much of that variance.
changes.after: Independent fluctuations partly cancel in the average. Shared fluctuations move every channel together, so the average moves with them and does not shrink by the square root of N.

changes.after: Its +10 Hz vote becomes 0, so the vertical component falls from 20 to 10. The vector still points up and right but is shorter and tilted toward right: the readout degrades rather than fails.

changes.before: A linear decoder (often fit with ridge regression) is still one of the most widely deployed decoding approaches in clinical and research BCIs because it is fast, interpretable, and robust when training data is limited. Seeing and changing the weights turns the decoder from magic into an engineering object you can debug and constrain.
changes.after: A weighted linear decoder is still widely used because it is fast, needs little data and can be inspected. Inspection only helps if you know what a weight does and does not tell you, and if your accuracy number was measured honestly.

changes.before: score = w₁·f₁ + w₂·f₂ + … + b (often with L2 regularization / ridge). The weights are chosen (or adapted) so the score favors the correct intention. Held-out evaluation and direct weight inspection tell you whether the model generalized and which channels or features actually drive the output.
changes.after: A weighted linear decoder computes score = w·f + b over many features and applies a fixed rule to the score. Weights are usually fitted on training data, for example by least squares or ridge regression; ridge adds a penalty that keeps weights small when data are limited or features are correlated. Two habits make the result trustworthy. First, read contributions, not raw weights. A feature's contribution to the score is its weight times its value. A tiny weight on a feature measured in large units can matter more than a large weight on a feature measured in small units. Standardizing features to comparable scales before fitting makes weight sizes easier to compare. Second, keep three kinds of data apart. Training data choose the weights. Validation data choose between candidate settings, such as the ridge penalty or which features to keep. Test data are used once, after every choice is fixed, to estimate performance on new trials. Any choice made by looking at test results turns the test set into part of training, and the reported accuracy becomes optimistic. Accuracy on a few rows is also uncertain: 4/4 correct says little about the next hundred trials.

changes.before: Each feature casts a weighted vote. You can look at every vote, raise or lower any voter's influence, and immediately see the effect on both training and held-out performance. Regularization (ridge) keeps individual weights from becoming absurdly large on noisy neural data.
changes.after: Weights are exchange rates between each feature's units and the score. To see who is driving the decision, convert every feature into score units first, then compare.

changes.before: Features = [left_rate=5, right_rate=11]. With w_left=-0.9, w_right=1.4, bias=-2.0 the score is positive → 'right'. After training you inspect the weights: the large positive w_right tells you the right-side feature is the dominant driver. If a channel's weight is near zero, you can often drop or mask it with little loss.
changes.after: Features: firing rate f0 in Hz and RMS f1 in µV. Weights [0.05, 4.0], bias -3. Trial [40 Hz, 0.3 µV]: contributions are 0.05 × 40 = 2.0 and 4.0 × 0.3 = 1.2, so the score is 2.0 + 1.2 - 3 = 0.2, labeled right. The rate drives the decision more, although its weight is 80 times smaller. If you choose among 20 candidate weight vectors by their accuracy on 4 test rows and report the best, that number is no longer a test result; a fresh, untouched set is needed. All values are synthetic.

changes.before: In any chronically implanted BCI, the relationship between neural activity and the features you extract will change over days and weeks. Understanding why and how to respond is one of the most important real-world engineering skills.
changes.after: Recalibrating from scratch every day costs the user time and attention. Adaptive systems try to keep the decoder aligned with the smallest, safest update that fixes the observed change.

changes.before: Drift has physical and statistical causes: electrode micromotion, gliosis/encapsulation (impedance rise), reference changes, and behavioral or learning-induced shifts. Different signatures (global offset, per-channel gain, tuning rotation / covariate shift) call for different responses. Good systems first detect the change (performance drop, confidence distribution shift, impedance rise) then apply the cheapest fix that restores control: baseline/gain correction, per-channel re-weighting, or a lightweight recursive update (e.g., exponential moving average on the weights or features). Full supervised re-fits or more sophisticated continual learning are used when cheap methods fail.
changes.after: Online adaptation updates decoder parameters during or between sessions. A useful ladder runs from cheap to expensive. First, per-channel offsets: re-estimate each channel's resting mean from a short rest block, with no labels. Second, per-channel scales: re-estimate how much each channel moves with intent, which needs a short block with known targets. Third, the weights themselves: a full recalibration. Normalizing each feature as (value - resting mean) / scale lets the weights stay fixed while offsets and scales are updated. A slow tracker can follow gradual change without stopping the user. An exponential moving average updates a running estimate m toward each new value x by a fraction a: m_new = m + a × (x - m). Small a changes slowly and resists noise; large a follows quickly but also follows anything else. That is the risk of unsupervised tracking: if the user holds one intention for a long time, the tracker can absorb it into the "baseline" and weaken the very command the user is producing. Published approaches range from self-recalibration during use (Jarosiewicz et al., 2015) and closed-loop decoder adaptation (Orsborn et al., 2014) to aligning low-dimensional neural activity across days (Degenhart et al., 2020).

changes.before: The mapping from neural activity to intent is not stationary. You must detect when it has changed and respond with the smallest intervention that keeps the user in control. A simple recursive update (exponential moving average on the weight vector or per-channel baseline) can track slow drift without forcing the user into frequent explicit recalibration sessions.
changes.after: Tune the instrument before you rewrite the music. Fix offsets, then scales, and rewrite the weights only when the tune itself has changed.

changes.before: After 6 weeks, channel 7 shows rising impedance and flattened tuning. A per-channel gain correction restores most performance. You also maintain a slow exponential moving average on the weight vector (learning rate ~0.01) that continuously tracks gradual changes across the population. When performance remains poor after the cheap fixes, you trigger a short supervised recalibration.

Updating only the mean gives (36 - 26) / 20 = 0.5. Updating the scale to today's 10 Hz modulation gives (36 - 26) / 10 = 1.0 again, with the weights untouched. before.prompt: When would you choose a lightweight baseline/gain correction or recursive update versus triggering a full supervised re-fit?

changes.before: Treating every performance drop as 'the electrodes failed' and assuming only surgery or total retraining can help. Most of the time a principled, minimal correction is sufficient.
changes.after: Refitting every weight whenever performance drops, or letting an unsupervised tracker run with no check on what it is absorbing.

changes.before: Every extra millisecond of latency changes both the user's strategy and the statistics the decoder must learn. Timing is a first-class design variable.
changes.after: Every stage between a neural event and the cursor adds delay. In a feedback loop, delay does more than slow things down: corrections based on old information keep pushing after they should stop, and the cursor overshoots.

changes.before: Real wireless high-channel BCIs target end-to-end latencies often below 80–120 ms from neural event to output (cursor movement or stimulation). Every filtering stage, wireless hop, and decoding step consumes the budget. Added latency forces the user to predict further ahead, changes the statistics the decoder must learn, and often makes slower, larger modulations more effective than fast ones.
changes.after: End-to-end latency is the time from a change in neural activity to a visible change in the output. It is a budget made of stages: the length of the window used to compute features, filtering, decoding, transmission, and the display refresh. Some stages are fixed costs; others are design choices. Shorter feature windows reduce delay but contain fewer spikes, so rate estimates get noisier. In a closed loop, delay changes behavior. The person corrects toward the target based on where the cursor appears to be. If that view is old, the correction continues after the cursor has already arrived, and the cursor overshoots and swings back. A lower controller gain reduces overshoot but makes movement sluggish. Cunningham and colleagues (2011) built a closed-loop simulator to study exactly these interactions between decoder, delay and human feedback. People also adapt. In monkeys using a BCI, Golub and colleagues (2015) found neural activity consistent with an internal model that partly compensates for feedback delay, and the feedback control of people using intracortical BCIs has been modeled directly (Willett and colleagues, 2017). Compensation is partial, so engineers still treat latency as a budget to defend.

changes.before: The cursor is always a little bit in the past. The user learns to aim where the cursor will be, not where it is. The decoder must therefore learn the user's predictive strategy, not their instantaneous intent.
changes.after: Steering by a video feed that is a fifth of a second behind. You keep turning after you are already lined up, then have to turn back.

changes.before: At 80 ms latency the user can still use relatively fast changes in firing rate. At 250 ms the same user starts producing slower, more deliberate modulations because fast corrections arrive too late.
changes.after: A synthetic budget: 50 ms feature window, 5 ms filter, 2 ms decode, 10 ms radio link, up to 17 ms waiting for a 60 Hz display refresh. Total: 50 + 5 + 2 + 10 + 17 = 84 ms. With a 100 ms budget, 16 ms remain. A cursor moving at 2 units/s travels 2 × 0.084 = 0.168 units during that delay. Now a toy loop: the cursor moves toward a target at 1.0 with velocity 5 × (target - observed position), updated every 0.1 s. Without delay the positions are 0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875: the error halves each step. If the observed position is 0.2 s old, the positions are 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 1.75, 1.5: the cursor passes the target and comes back.

changes.after: Why does delay cause overshoot rather than just a slower approach?

changes.before: They have to plan further ahead.
changes.after: What position is the correction based on?

changes.before: Fast corrections become useless; the user learns to make bigger, earlier changes that the delayed feedback can still influence.
changes.after: The correction uses an old position that still looks short of the target, so it keeps pushing after the real cursor has arrived.

changes.before: If you can only spend engineering effort on one thing — better features or 40 ms lower latency — which one usually gives more bit-rate in a real cursor task?
changes.after: Halving the feature window from 100 ms to 50 ms cuts latency. What does it cost for a spike-count feature?

changes.before: Latency is brutally expensive.
changes.after: Count how many spikes fit in each window.

changes.before: Lower latency almost always wins at the margin because it changes the user's strategy and the statistics of the problem itself.
changes.after: Fewer spikes per window, so each rate estimate is noisier. Latency and noise trade against each other.

changes.before: Treating latency as a pure engineering annoyance instead of a variable that reshapes the neural signals the decoder must learn.
changes.after: Treating latency as a single number to report instead of a budget whose stages trade against noise and controller gain.

changes.after: You can add up a latency budget, state what each stage trades away, and explain with numbers why delayed feedback makes a cursor overshoot.

changes.before: A decoder that occasionally acts when it should not can be worse than one that sometimes refuses to act. Confidence and graceful degradation are safety and trust features, not UI polish.
changes.after: A decoder that must answer every window will act on its weakest evidence. Letting it say "not sure" can prevent many wrong actions, at the price of acting less often.

changes.before: When the evidence is weak or contradictory, a good system slows down, widens its acceptance window, or explicitly asks the user for confirmation instead of guessing and being wrong.
changes.after: A linear score carries more than its sign: a score near the threshold rests on weak evidence, while one far away rests on strong evidence, at least for the data the decoder was fitted on. An abstain rule turns that into a third output. Within a margin around the threshold the decoder abstains; outside it, it labels as usual. Two numbers then describe performance. Coverage is the fraction of windows on which the system acts. Selective accuracy is the accuracy among those acted windows. Widening the margin usually raises selective accuracy and lowers coverage. Distance from the threshold is not a calibrated probability: a score can be far from the threshold and still be wrong, for example when drift moved the features. Calibration methods map scores to probabilities that can be checked against outcomes. Graceful degradation is the plan for when abstaining persists. A system that has abstained for several seconds should hold still, say plainly that it is unsure, and offer a recalibration or another input rather than quietly lowering its standards. Abstaining is a decision layer; how the interface shows uncertainty is the subject of Unit 17.

changes.before: The system has a 'I am not sure' state. In that state it asks for help or does nothing rather than risking a costly mistake.
changes.after: A careful driver at a confusing junction slows down and checks before turning. Stopping is a real option, not a failure, but stopping forever is not driving either. The margin sets how confusing a junction has to be before the driver stops.

changes.before: If the linear score is only +0.3 (just above threshold) the cursor moves very slowly or the interface pops up 'Confirm right?'. The user can cancel or strengthen the command.
changes.after: Ten synthetic windows, threshold 0, right above 0. Scores [2.1, 1.4, 0.3, -0.2, -1.8, -2.5, 0.4, -0.4, 1.9, -1.1]; true labels [R, R, L, R, L, L, R, L, L, L]. Acting on all ten gives 7 correct; counting from 1, windows 3, 4 and 9 are wrong. With a margin of 0.5, windows 3, 4, 7 and 8 abstain, because their scores are within 0.5 of 0. The six acted windows give 5 correct: selective accuracy 5/6 ≈ 83 % at 60 % coverage. Two errors were avoided, two correct actions were lost, and window 9 is still a confident error.

changes.before: What is the difference between 'the decoder is uncertain' and 'the user changed their mind'?
changes.after: Why is a score far from the threshold not proof that the label is correct?

changes.before: One is epistemic, one is intentional.
changes.after: Look at window 9 in the worked example.

changes.before: Uncertainty means the neural evidence is weak or noisy. Mind change means the user now wants the opposite action. Good interfaces try to distinguish the two.
changes.after: Distance only reflects the fitted rule. Drift, artifacts or a poor fit can produce confident wrong scores; only checking against outcomes shows whether confidence is calibrated.

changes.before: Why can a system that 'always does something' actually reduce the user's sense of control?
changes.after: What should an interface do after the decoder has abstained for several seconds?

changes.before: Wrong actions feel like loss of agency.
changes.after: Think about the user's experience and options.

changes.before: Every incorrect action teaches the user that the device sometimes acts against their will. Occasional explicit 'I don't know' states preserve trust.
changes.after: Hold still, say clearly that it is unsure, and offer a recalibration or an alternative input. It should not quietly shrink the margin to start acting again.

changes.before: Optimizing only for accuracy or speed while ignoring the user's subjective experience of being in control.
changes.after: Forcing a label on every window, or hiding persistent uncertainty by quietly shrinking the margin.

changes.before: You can design simple confidence-aware behaviors and explain why they improve both objective performance and user trust.
changes.after: You can apply an abstain margin by hand, compute coverage and selective accuracy, and describe a graceful-degradation policy that keeps the user informed.

changes.before: When the output of the BCI can cause physical effects (stimulation, movement, speech), the cost of errors is no longer symmetric. Safety engineering becomes a first-class requirement.
changes.after: When an output stimulates tissue or moves a limb, the two kinds of error stop being equally bad. Safety engineering makes the harmful error rare by design rather than by hoping the detector is accurate.

changes.before: False positives and false negatives now have real physiological or functional costs. Systems must be designed so that dangerous mistakes are orders of magnitude harder than useful actions. Key controls include charge-density and charge-balance limits per stimulation phase, rate limiting on commands, explicit user interlocks that cannot be overridden by the algorithm, and fail-safe states. Chronic drift can silently move a previously safe operating point into the danger region if detection and compensation are missing.
changes.after: Start by pricing the errors. If a false positive and a false negative have different costs, the best threshold is the one with the lowest expected cost: false positives times their cost plus false negatives times theirs. The costs are clinical and personal judgments made with clinicians and users, not values the code can discover. Then add layers that do not rely on the detector being right. Confirmation requires the condition to persist, for example several consecutive windows above threshold, before acting; it filters brief artifacts and adds a known delay. Rate limits cap how often the system may act. Hard limits bound the output itself: for electrical stimulation, charge per phase and charge density are kept inside ranges such as those described by Shannon's model of safe levels (1992) and in reviews of safe protocol design (Merrill et al., 2005). Interlocks let the user or a separate circuit stop the output regardless of what the algorithm decides. A fail-safe default means a fault leads to a safe state, usually no output. Finally, drift can move a safe operating point: a threshold that produced few false actions last month can produce many after the signal shifts.

changes.before: The system has two very different error budgets: one for 'missed useful action' and one for 'harmful action'. The second budget is tiny — and drift can silently move a previously safe system across that line.
changes.after: Two error budgets: a generous one for missed help and a tiny one for harm. Every layer you add should protect the tiny budget even when the detector is wrong.

changes.before: A seizure-detection stimulator was tuned with a threshold that produced <1 false positive per week on month-1 data. By month-3, electrode impedance rise and a small baseline shift on one channel cause the same threshold to trigger 40 unnecessary stimulations per day. The team must either raise the threshold (risking missed events) or add drift compensation + an explicit confirmation step before stimulation.
changes.after: Two synthetic thresholds over one day. Threshold A: 40 false positives, 1 false negative. Threshold B: 6 false positives, 3 false negatives. If a false positive costs 1 and a false negative costs 10, A costs 40 + 10 = 50 and B costs 6 + 30 = 36, so B is better. If a false negative costs 20, A costs 40 + 20 = 60 and B costs 6 + 60 = 66, so A is better. The data did not change; the cost judgment did. Confirmation: requiring 3 consecutive 100 ms windows above threshold means acting at the end of the third window, 200 ms after the first one ended.

before.prompt: Why is a 99 % accurate detector still dangerous if the 1 % errors are all false positives that trigger stimulation?
before.answer: One percent of 10 000 daily detections is 100 unnecessary stimulations — potentially unacceptable.

before.prompt: What is the simplest 'interlock' that prevents a closed-loop system from acting while the user is explicitly overriding?
before.answer: A button, voice command, or eye-tracking 'stop' signal that the user can assert faster than the automatic loop can act.

before.prompt: How can undetected drift turn a previously safe closed-loop system into an unsafe one?
before.answer: Features that used to indicate 'no stimulation needed' can drift into the stimulation region. Without drift detection or compensation, the system will now over-stimulate on what used to be normal activity.

after.prompt: Why can the code not choose the costs of each error type?
after.answer: The costs depend on clinical effects and the person's values. They have to be agreed with clinicians and users and then written into the design.

after.prompt: Which safety layer still works if the detection algorithm has a bug?
after.hint: Look for layers outside the algorithm.
after.answer: A hard limit on the output or an independent interlock, because neither depends on the detector deciding correctly.

changes.before: Optimizing the detector in isolation and only later discovering that its operating point is unsafe in the real clinical context.
changes.after: Tuning the detector for accuracy alone and adding safety limits after the operating point has been chosen.

changes.before: You can reason about asymmetric error costs and propose at least one concrete safety mechanism (threshold, confirmation, interlock, or override) for a closed-loop neurotechnology application, including how drift could invalidate yesterday's safety assumptions.
changes.after: You can compare thresholds by expected cost, explain what a confirmation window buys and costs, and name a safety layer that does not depend on the detector.

changes.before: Neural data is uniquely sensitive because it supports inference about unstated mental states. Architecture, consent, and re-identification risk must be designed in from day one.
changes.after: Where computation happens decides which data ever leave the device, and every change to a medical device's software has to be controlled and documented. Both are architecture decisions, not paperwork added at the end.

changes.before: Raw neural recordings or high-dimensional feature vectors can be re-identified or used to infer attention, emotion, or intent. On-device processing, data minimization, and explicit consent versioning are not optional. Adding unsupervised drift compensation can constitute a software change that requires risk re-analysis and documentation under design controls (IEC 62304, 21 CFR 820). Wireless implants also face cybersecurity expectations. Chronic drift is therefore both an engineering and a regulatory fact of life.
changes.after: A BCI pipeline spans places: the implant or headset, a body-worn or bedside processor, a phone or computer, and perhaps a cloud service. Each boundary is a point where data can be exposed, so a good architecture computes as much as possible before the boundary and sends only what the next stage needs. Raw recordings are hard to anonymize: removing a name leaves high-dimensional signals and metadata that may be linked back to a person, so removing identifiers is pseudonymization at best. Consent should be versioned, with each record tagged by the consent version that covered it, so that a later research export can include only records whose consent allowed that use. Regulation adds its own constraints. In the United States, the FDA has published recommendations for implanted BCI devices covering non-clinical testing and clinical study design, and expects manufacturers to address cybersecurity across a device's life. Changes to device software, including an adaptive algorithm that changes decoder behavior, fall under design controls and may need validation before release. In the EU, the GDPR treats health data as a special category. Which rules apply depends on the product, its claims and the jurisdiction, so engineers work with regulatory specialists from the start.

changes.before: Every piece of neural data you store or transmit is a potential future liability or a future research asset. You must decide which it will be before you collect it — and drift means the system you validated yesterday may no longer behave the same way tomorrow.
changes.after: Draw a line around each device. Every arrow that crosses a line is a promise to the user about what leaves, why, and who can read it.

changes.before: A wellness BCI that uploads raw LFP to the cloud for 'better decoding' also uploads enough information to potentially infer the user's mood, attention, or even some disease markers. That upload now requires a different consent flow and stronger technical protections. If the team later adds automatic drift compensation that changes the effective decoder behavior, they may also trigger additional change-control documentation under software-as-medical-device rules.
changes.after: A synthetic headset records 1 s windows at 1,000 samples per second. Instead of sending 1,000 samples, the device sends three numbers per window: the sample count, the number of threshold episodes and the RMS. For the short window [0, 3, 4, 0, 5] with threshold 2 those numbers are 5, 2 and the square root of (0 + 9 + 16 + 0 + 25) / 5 = 10, about 3.16. Consent: of 800 stored records, 500 were collected under consent version 1 (decoding only) and 300 under version 2 (decoding and research). A research export may include only the 300.

before.prompt: Why is 'we'll just anonymize the neural data later' usually not a credible plan?
before.hint: High-dimensional data is hard to anonymize.
before.answer: Neural signals are high-dimensional and individual. Simple de-identification is often reversible with auxiliary information.

before.prompt: What is the practical difference between training a decoder on-device versus sending data to the cloud?
before.hint: Raw data exposure and attack surface.
before.answer: On-device keeps the raw signal (and therefore the most sensitive inferences) inside the user's physical device. Cloud training requires either sending raw data or using federated / privacy-preserving techniques.

before.prompt: Why can unhandled chronic drift create a regulatory or change-control burden even if the underlying hardware has not changed?
before.answer: If drift compensation or automatic re-weighting meaningfully alters the decoder's input-output relationship, the system may be considered to have undergone a software change that requires documentation, risk re-analysis, or even re-validation depending on the regulatory jurisdiction.

after.prompt: Why is "we removed the names" not the same as anonymizing raw neural recordings?
after.hint: What else in the data could identify someone?
after.answer: High-dimensional signals and their metadata may be linkable to a person with other information. Removing names is pseudonymization, which reduces but does not remove the risk.

after.prompt: Why should each stored record carry the consent version it was collected under?
after.answer: So that each later use can be checked against what the person actually agreed to when that record was collected.

changes.before: Treating privacy and regulatory requirements as paperwork that happens after the product is built.
changes.after: Uploading raw data by default and planning to anonymize or obtain consent afterwards.

changes.before: The final skill is not building one more algorithm. It is integrating everything you have learned into a coherent, documented toy system and then honestly describing exactly why that toy is still far from a real clinical device — especially the realities of chronic non-stationarity.
changes.after: Each unit built one stage. Engineering a system means connecting the stages so that every handoff has a defined input, output and unit, and then saying plainly what the whole thing still cannot do.

changes.before: The Unit 20 capstone is the disciplined assembly of a full toy pipeline (raw signal → feature vector → weighted linear decoder → latency-aware feedback) plus a concise, technically honest reflection. The reflection must name at least two distinct mechanisms of chronic non-stationarity (e.g., impedance rise + gliosis, tuning rotation), describe one detection method and one practical response (baseline correction, recursive update, or selective re-fit), one safety or regulatory implication of that response, and the single most important concrete next engineering step a real team would staff tomorrow.
changes.after: The capstone chains four stages you have already built. Baseline subtraction removes each channel's resting level. Threshold-episode counting turns each corrected channel into a count, using the rule from Unit 2. A weighted linear score with an explicit tie rule turns the two counts into a label. A cursor step moves a fixed distance for each label. Integration work is mostly about contracts. Each stage should state its input, its output, the units and what happens at boundaries, such as a sample exactly at threshold, a score of exactly zero or an empty trial. A fixed input with known expected outputs, a regression test, tells you when a change breaks something. Returning intermediate values (features, labels, positions) lets you find which stage caused a wrong final answer. Passing that test establishes that the code computes the authored outputs for that input. It does not establish that the pipeline decodes intent from real recordings. The toy omits realistic noise, sorting, drift, latency, a human learning in the loop, safety interlocks and clinical validation. Naming those gaps precisely, with the mechanism and the first test you would run, is part of the engineering, not an apology for it.

changes.before: You have built a working toy BCI. Now you must also be able to explain, in one clear page, why no patient would receive this exact system tomorrow — with specific mechanisms of drift, not slogans — and what the real next engineering or clinical step would be.
changes.after: An assembly line with an inspection window after every station. When the final product is wrong, you look through the windows to find the station, not at the product.
